utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case number IT-98-32-T, the Prosecutor versus Mitar Vasiljevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: While we are waiting for the witnesses to return, Mr. Domazet, I understand you've got a report at last.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Have you served it?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have not because I left a message this morning for Mr. Loran ^ to say that I was in the Defence room, to hand it to him, however, he didn't turn up before the trial began so that I have it. I have the report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Anyway, you're going to file it today, are you?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, at the first opportunity during the first break, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Now, have you got -- sorry, is there something you want to add?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do, Your Honour. Before the witness enters the courtroom, I should like to say something, that is to say, the Defence has a comment to make, a criticism to make with respect to the procedure regarding the Defence witnesses last week. Most -- although I am well aware of the fact that it is the task of cross-examination, in addition to referring to the examination-in-chief topics and the credibility of the witness, I think that quoting portions of certain statements which are by unidentified witnesses who have not testified in this case with respect to the Defence witnesses testifying here is something which can upset the proceedings and have consequences on the Defence case. That is to say, witnesses can either refuse to come to testify or refuse to come to the Tribunal at all to testify, because I think the manner in which the Prosecution examines some of the witnesses or, rather, most of the witnesses during their cross-examination was, in the opinion of the Defence, untenable. It's surpassed the -- what is allowed for the credibility of witnesses. Some witnesses were directly asked whether they had taken part in killings, and this was done in such a way that they were quoted they had -- they had quotations held at them from sources that we don't know where they are, whether they existed at all or whether they had come up in the course of this trial at all. So I should like to discuss that particular matter before we go ahead with the Defence witnesses because I fear that this might have serious repercussions on the trial and it would jeopardize our intention and desire to have this trial be a fair trial in an atmosphere of equitable relations. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: But Mr. Domazet, there are two matters that you raise. One was the use of unidentified witness statements saying, "We have a statement that says," and that, I must say, was something which I had never seen before and I did not think that it was appropriate, but perhaps Mr. Groome has got some justification for it. But the other point, I'm not sure that I understand where you -- where you stand. If Mr. Groome had simply said, "I want to put to you that you were involved in the killing of a number of people on a bus," and then gave the details, without having said that it was in a statement, how could that not go to the witness' credit? It also, as I understand it, goes to one of the -- went to one of the incidents upon which the Prosecution relies to establish an attack upon the civilian population. So it went to an issue in the case as well as to credit. Is the only objection you're taking the use of -- or the reference to statements? Because if that is the burden of your complaint, I understand it, and subject to anything Mr. Groome says, I agree with it. But you cannot stop a party cross-examining your witness on credit, and credit may involve matters as serious as being involved in the killings of people.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I fully agree, Your Honour. My criticism was the reading out of the statements which could create in public, as this is a public trial, it might lead the public to surmise and conject that there were -- was evidence to that effect. Where -- I am not questioning the right of the Prosecution, not only Mr. Groome but the entire Prosecution, to ask any questions which it wants to regarding witness credibility, but I don't think that they can use completely unknown portions, not even full statements, but portions of statements of witnesses that have not testified here. So that is the gist of what I wanted to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, Mr. Groome, I of course grew up, as you did, in a jury system of criminal trials. If you had asked those questions in a trial in Australia, the jury would probably have been discharged. What is the purpose of referring to the fact that the allegation you are putting to the witness in cross-examination comes from a statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, simply to make clear that I have obviously have no personal knowledge of the events that I'm inquiring of this witness and that the source of my information is from a statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: But it carries with it the implication that there is evidence of that fact, and there is no evidence of that fact in some of the ones you did. There was in others. But may I suggest to you that your concern about it is not being of your knowledge, is something you can use if proceedings are taken against you for some unethical conduct, but it is, if I may say so, gravely wrong to assert that you have a statement. What do you say about it? Witnesses are not entitled to be asked -- I'm sorry, parties are not entitled to ask witnesses to comment upon other evidence, but the allegation can be put to them and put to them squarely. And the way you do it, the way in which something more than 40 years of experience has taught me, you say, "I want to suggest to you that you did so and so." Now, that's the proper way of doing it, and may I suggest you follow that in future.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I will, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: All right. Well, all right, now let's get on with Witness VGD23.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm going to ask that the witness be shown a copy of Defence Exhibit 22.1.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Cross-examined by Mr. Groome: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness VGD23, I'm going to ask you to look at that list and ask you to indicate which of those names you recognise. If you do recognise a name, I would ask you at this stage not to tell us that name but rather refer to that person by the number to the left of their name. So for example, if you recognise the first name on the list, you would say that you recognise VGD3. Are we clear?

utterances.speaker: Witness VGD23 [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No audible response]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd ask you to look down that list and when you've finished, would you tell us which of those people -- which of those people's names you recognise?

utterances.speaker: Witness VGD23 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recognise VGD10, VGD12, VGD15, VGD16, VGD17, VGD18, VGD19. That's all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, when you say you recognise these names, are these people that you personally know?

utterances.speaker: Witness VGD23 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Aside from these people that you personally know, are there any other names on this list who you've heard of or have had some dealings with, with respect to your job as a [redacted]?

utterances.speaker: Witness VGD23 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The other names don't. I heard about the surnames. I did hear of some of the surnames but I can't say anything specific with regard to the name and surname. I recognise some of the surnames. I know that there are families like [redacted] and so on in Visegrad but not the names, first names.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There's been testimony by a Defence witness that some of the names on this list are men that were involved in paramilitary activity in the Visegrad area. Are either of the names of the people you know or the other names, do you recognise any of these names as being associated with, or any of these people, as being associated with paramilitary activity in the town of Visegrad?

utterances.speaker: Witness VGD23 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know any of these people as having been in any paramilitary units.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were any of the people that you've indicated you know on this list, were any of them present in the escort that you provided for that bus past Olovo?

utterances.speaker: Witness VGD23 [Resumed]
utterances.text: None of the ones here was with me in the escort for the convoy.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There was some testimony earlier in this trial from a survivor of another convoy, again describing an attack upon Bosnian Muslim men, and it was in the same area as you described the convoy that you were part of. Had you ever heard about other convoys of Bosnian Muslims being taken from Visegrad and some of those people being killed before they arrived where that convoy was allegedly supposed to go?

utterances.speaker: Witness VGD23 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did hear about a convoy and before my convoy, the convoy I escorted, it wasn't taking people away, it was just escorting them, but there were convoys after my particular convoy, but I didn't hear anything about any attacks on Bosnian males, Muslim Bosnian males. But when I took on my assignment together with the other members of the team to escort the convoy to Olovo, I understood the seriousness of the situation and I knew the risk I personally was taking, the members of my team were taking on. Let me also mention the risk the driver took, the drivers driving those buses and trucks, and especially for the women and children who were in the convoy. So that on the journey, I saw on their faces and in their eyes that they were full of fear. I tried to help them overcome their fear, although I did know that we were passing through untapped territory, and they told us that we would be using some byroads to some Serb villages and through some Serb villages which were probably controlled by Serbian forces, but this did not exclude the possibility of paramilitary formations, both Serb and Muslim, intersecting the roads. I said to them, "Well I'm with you, the drivers are with you. If anybody shoots at the buses and vehicles, they'll kill me too and you, so we're in the same position. And I am here to try and assure you that we will get to our destination safely." And let me stress that in the bus, a male who was blind was killed. He was about 60 years old, a blind man, and I think that that happened because the rest of the passengers got out and probably were taking out some things, their things from the buses, and he stayed on the bus and they should have gone back for him. So those people who had set the ambush and prepared the attack for us, they probably thought that all of us had got off the buses, and they wanted to incapacitate the buses and trucks so they would be able to overcome us easier, more easily afterwards. So I think that we were lucky in getting out alive, us and the drivers and all the other people, except for the two people who were killed. We were all alive and well. I think that God repaid us for the humane thing we were doing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So none of the escort team was injured in any way; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Witness VGD23 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, none of the escorts or the drivers, although one driver did receive a wound from a hunting weapon which would make it 12 times 12 calibre, a brener type that is used in a hunting weapon. So it actually -- actually, it hit the door by the driver, whizzed passed the driver and lodged somewhere behind the driver, but actually the driver was not hurt.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's mistake, the driver was not hurt.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it your testimony that the people who were killed that day were killed from the gunfire from this elevated area you referred to or were they killed from fire from the escort when they returned the fire to the people who were shooting at the escort?

utterances.speaker: Witness VGD23 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, nobody could have been killed by the escort because the vehicles were behind our backs so the attack came from the frontal part where the area is flat and then the elevation comes after that. And so all of the passengers who were not able to get far away from the vehicle were right by that little hill. They were hiding behind it. I was there, Hecimovic was next to me. I can't -- I can't remember his first name. I know he is Hamdo Hecimovic's father, and he said, "Neighbour, what's this happening to us?" And I think that all the passengers without exception, at least that is how I experienced it with the -- they were very grateful to us, from what I could see on their faces, because they understood what risk we had taken with our lives to enable them to be secure and to arrive at their destination unharmed and safely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So after this attack, did you put the people back into the bus and take them to their destination safely?

utterances.speaker: Witness VGD23 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not all of them, a part of them. I can't tell you exactly how many, a smaller portion of the people, out of fear, had gone back into either one or two of the buses, I can't remember now. I think it was -- they went back into two buses, and those passengers, together with us, reached Sokolac and that's where we saw that two passengers were dead, the blind man that I mentioned and another woman.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you agree with me that it is possible that some of the other people that had fled the buses and into the woods surrounding the buses may also have been killed and you were not aware of it from your own personal knowledge; correct?

utterances.speaker: Witness VGD23 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you return fire that day to these people that were firing at you from the elevated position?

utterances.speaker: Witness VGD23 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say that all of them did return fire. Two or three men, perhaps, shot two or three bullets in the direction of a hill.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you return fire?

utterances.speaker: Witness VGD23 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I shot two or three bullets, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it possible that you shot some of these Muslim people by accident when you were returning fire; is that a possibility?

utterances.speaker: Witness VGD23 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it your --

utterances.speaker: Witness VGD23 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, there is absolutely no possibility of that having happened because I did not fire at any target. It was more up in -- upwards as a warning, up in the air as a warning. So I didn't actually target anyone, so I am 100 per cent certain that I could not even have hit a bird, let alone a man.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the other shots fired by the members of your escort squad, did they also fire their shots as warning shots up into the air?

utterances.speaker: Witness VGD23 [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we arrived in Sokolac and after that event, when they analysed the situation, they told me that they had also shot up in the air as warning shots, and the passengers who had already been -- who had already got off the buses screamed out, "Don't shoot. They're women and children. Don't shoot, they're women and children." And we were conscious, at least I was 100 per cent conscious of the fact that if they were to open stronger fire -- if we were to open fire more, they would have reacted and that there would have been many more casualties than there were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you estimate for us for how long a period of time this fire came from the elevated position or how many shots were fired, if that's an easier way for you to estimate the character of the fight that you were up against?

utterances.speaker: Witness VGD23 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I couldn't tell you how long it went on for because, you know, time flies in situations like that or perhaps time is very slow in moments like that -- at moments like that, so I can't really say how long it went on for, but it wasn't very strong gunfire without intermission. It wasn't strong bursts of gunfire but it was shots here and there aimed at the buses and trucks and the transport vehicles, actually.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it's your testimony here today that this fire that was coming at you that was hitting the bus behind you killed at least two people that you are aware of, that in light of that kind of attack upon you and the people you were trying to protect, no one in the escort team fired anything other than warning shots? Is that what you're telling us here today?

utterances.speaker: Witness VGD23 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I couldn't do anything more than that because they were shooting from the hill. We had taken cover behind this embankment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And from what you're telling us, it appears that upon hearing these warning shots, whoever it was, however many men decided to attack you and the convoy, upon hearing these warning shoots, they ceased their attack, allowed you to load up some of the people back into the bus and to continue on your way; is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: Witness VGD23 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, it lasted a short period of time. The bus drivers and truck drivers jumped into their buses and trucks and they began shouting out, "Jump into the bus. Come on board." And although I was in the first bus to begin with, I managed to jump into the last bus. And had I not reacted so quickly, the drivers who were afraid themselves would have left me there. They wouldn't have actually even realised that they had left me behind, perhaps. So I had to, regardless of what was going on, I had to jump into the bus. Otherwise, I would have stayed behind at the mercy of the people who were shooting from up above.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And as soon as the people were in the bus, the bus took off to try to get to a safer area; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Witness VGD23 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you've told us several times you were the first person in the bus. You haven't mentioned anything about any obstacle or any tree being across the road, so can you describe for us why it was your bus, the first bus, stopped in the first place?

utterances.speaker: Witness VGD23 [Resumed]
utterances.text: We arrived at the spot where the passengers were supposed to get out. We had a guide in Knezina Sokolac, too, in fact who knew the area because neither us escorts or the drivers knew the road from Knezina onwards, so we got these two guides and they took us and they said you have to go through the woods, but there is a plateau there, a wider space where the buses could -- and trucks could turn around and the passengers from the convoy could get off and carry on, on foot, and the buses could turn around, because there is a Muslim settlement nearby, not far off, and that part was controlled by Muslim forces so that would mean that the passengers could go on foot to that area and they would enter an area of the Olovo municipality. So we had reached the spot where we were supposed to get to and there was no obstacle there, nor were there any obstacles along the road. We just stopped once on our way where we saw that there was some water, so I got out and two or three younger women got out, we took some water, we took bottles and filled them with water for the children and the elderly, and that's what happened. We asked anybody whether they needed to be excused, go to the toilet, and that was all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm getting confused now. If this is the final destination of the people, why is it necessary for some people to be allowed to use the toilet and others to collect water? If this is where you are dropping the people off and they are going to continue on foot from there, this sounds more in the nature of a break; isn't that -- why is there a necessity to have people use the toilet and to get water if this is the final destination?

utterances.speaker: Witness VGD23 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think you understood me or it wasn't properly interpreted. I said, "On the way from Visegrad, somewhere before Sokolac," that's where we stopped to -- on the right-hand side, there was water so it was on the way. It wasn't at the destination. It wasn't when we got to our destination. There wasn't any water there or anything, it was on the way before reaching Sokolac that this happened, en route.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me ask you this: The driver of the bus you were in was a Serb; correct?

utterances.speaker: Witness VGD23 [Resumed]
utterances.text: All drivers were Serbs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was the name of the bus company that provided the transportation?

utterances.speaker: Witness VGD23 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Visegradtrans.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, did you assist in the organisation of the buses that were going to be used in this convoy?

utterances.speaker: Witness VGD23 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who did that?

utterances.speaker: Witness VGD23 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, who contacted you and asked you to provide the security for this convoy?

utterances.speaker: Witness VGD23 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dragan Tomic, the chief of the police station.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I asked you last week about whether or not you had anything to do with the detention of Muslims, and let me put it to you, sir, isn't it a fact that you were actually had a role of primary responsibility for those Muslims that had been detained by the police during the spring and summer of 1992; isn't that a fact?

utterances.speaker: Witness VGD23 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it isn't. I didn't have any such responsibility.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you aware of where Muslims were detained? Muslims that had been detained by police in Visegrad, are you aware of where they were detained?

utterances.speaker: Witness VGD23 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not remember a single case. I simply do not know that the police detained anyone at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would it be fair to say that you being a police officer, if Muslims were being detained on a regular basis, that you would have been aware of that fact; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Witness VGD23 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there is -- it is also possible that I wouldn't be aware of it because I wasn't always in town or, rather, I came to town very, very seldom. I spent most of my time in the field. As I said, I was providing security along the roads, and I seldom came to town, just to take a bath, for a change of clothing and get some rest before I would go back into the field, but I am simply not aware at all of such cases that you mention.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you give us an idea, what was the distance between the town and these areas where you worked, that you patrolled, how far out of the town were they?

utterances.speaker: Witness VGD23 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could be as many as 10 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where did you report in the morning to work or at the beginning of your shift at whatever time of the day that was, where did you report when you were reporting to work?

utterances.speaker: Witness VGD23 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not always in the morning. Sometimes it was in the afternoon or, at times, a time was not specified at all. I would report to the commander or he would send a driver to fetch me, to my place. For the sake of efficiency, he simply sends a driver, the driver gets to my home and he says, "We're off to a mission."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it's your testimony that rather than going to the police station, Dragan Tomic would send a driver to your home, pick you up, bring you to wherever Dragan Tomic wanted you to work that day and leave you there for your shift; is that correct? I'm sorry, can you please answer that question?

utterances.speaker: Witness VGD23 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never went on a mission by myself, alone. We were always in a group.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But am I correct in hearing what you are saying that Dragan Tomic would send a driver to pick up you and perhaps other men and bring them to wherever it was he wanted them to work for the day; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Witness VGD23 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The driver would take me to the police station and there, the rest of the group would also come together and then we'd take that vehicle to a particular section of the road. We would get off there and then provide the security for a section of the road, moving on foot.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is this the police station in Visegrad?

utterances.speaker: Witness VGD23 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So every day you would be brought to the police station in Visegrad, issued your orders and then you would go out to wherever you were going to patrol that day; correct?

utterances.speaker: Witness VGD23 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it is not. At times, we stayed seven, sometimes less, but also sometimes more days on the ground. We returned to town very seldom.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it's your testimony that at any time you were in the police station, you never saw any Muslims detained in that police station?

utterances.speaker: Witness VGD23 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I want to draw your attention to the 20th of April, 1992. Were you present with other soldiers in the village of Drinsko and there you were asking people to turn over their weapons? Do you recall ever being in Drinsko around the 20th of April, collecting weapons from people?

utterances.speaker: Witness VGD23 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you ever involved in the collection of weapons from people in Visegrad town?

utterances.speaker: Witness VGD23 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Isn't it a fact that you were present in Drinsko on that day and you demanded with the threat of force that the Muslims in that village turn over their weapons to you, many of those weapons for which people could produce valid licences for; isn't that a fact?

utterances.speaker: Witness VGD23 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, because I was not there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There's been testimony from two Defence witnesses regarding people being handed weapons early in the year of 1992, Serbs being given weapons during that period of time. Were you aware of any such instances of Serbs being provided weapons by the Serb authorities or, in particular, the SDS political party?

utterances.speaker: Witness VGD23 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not aware of any such case.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the course of your duties or outside of your duties, did you ever have occasion to search houses?

utterances.speaker: Witness VGD23 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Isn't it a fact that you searched the Podzic house - that's P-O-D-Z-I-C - that you searched the Podzic house in the spring of 1992; didn't you do that?

utterances.speaker: Witness VGD23 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not true. Not only spring of 1992, never.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, in your duties on protecting the highways, did you ever have any incident that you were involved in, in the course of your duties?

utterances.speaker: Witness VGD23 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand what incident do you have in mind, a traffic one or something else?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm asking you to describe for us any incident of a serious nature, not a minor traffic incident, but any incident of a serious nature which occurred on the roads that you were involved in while you were protecting or patrolling those roads.

utterances.speaker: Witness VGD23 [Resumed]
utterances.text: From 1992 onward; is that the period you're asking me about?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's confine ourselves to the spring and summer of 1992 for the moment.

utterances.speaker: Witness VGD23 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't involved in any incident.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have ever an occasion to use your weapon during the spring and summer of 1992?

utterances.speaker: Witness VGD23 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We ended on Friday with my asking you about an Ibrasim Kesmer, and I believe you said -- well, let me ask you, do you know that person? That person is from Drinsko as well?

utterances.speaker: Witness VGD23 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was born in the village of Drinsko, that is, in its hamlet, one of its hamlets, and the surname Kesmer never existed in Drinsko. I can affirm it and I can prove it. That name Ibrisim Kesmer, never. I know those people, perhaps not all of them, but I know all the surnames, the surnames of all the people living there and that surname, Kesmer, they never lived in the village of Drinsko, never.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, sir, can I take it from that then that it would be very unlikely from somebody from Drinsko to mistake you for somebody else if they were claiming that you had done something in Drinsko? That would be very unlikely that person would be mistaken since you, yourself, are from Drinsko; correct?

utterances.speaker: Witness VGD23 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know everybody, at least elderly people, I knew them all. So following the same logic, the majority of them should know me, too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me ask you this: I'm talking about an incident which occurred on the Visegrad bridge on the 25th of May - maybe give or take a day in either direction - 25th of May, 1992, when a large group of Muslims from Drinsko were crossing that bridge and came under fire at that time. Two of them were injured, Ibrisim Kesmer and his wife. Did you ever hear of that incident?

utterances.speaker: Witness VGD23 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not hear about it, and I repeat once again that Ibrisim Kesmer is not from Drinsko.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Isn't it a fact, sir, that after Ibrisim Kesmer and his wife were shot and lie wounded on the bridge, that you, yourself, pulled up alongside them and picked up both of them and put them into your car and drove away with them? Isn't that a fact?

utterances.speaker: Witness VGD23 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever place the bodies of two people that had been shot on one of the bridges in Visegrad into your car?

utterances.speaker: Witness VGD23 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Never.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know a person by the name of Midhat Tabakovic?

utterances.speaker: Witness VGD23 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever beat a person by that name and remove their pistol, a legally-owned pistol?

utterances.speaker: Witness VGD23 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We were told that an incident occurred in Sarajevo airport that involved you and somebody who recognised you in the airport. Can you describe for us your account of what occurred? What did that person accuse you of doing?

utterances.speaker: Witness VGD23 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's not that I was accused of it directly, but as we waited for the plane, and it could have been three hours, perhaps more, we approached the bar, three of us, Dikic, [redacted] and myself, to have a coffee. We were served by the barman, who looked at me and then asked me, "What was your name?" And when I gave him my last name, he then said my full name, my first and my last name. And then he said, "Aren't you ashamed? Shame on you, you've killed my brother. Pray to God that we met here. Had it been somewhere else, you'd be begging me for mercy," or something like that. He gave me his name. And all I said was, "What do we have to do with it?" So we finished our coffee and went back and sat over there, I mean where our bags and luggage were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That man was from Visegrad; correct?

utterances.speaker: Witness VGD23 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did he tell you how he knew or upon what he was basing his allegation that you had killed his brother?

utterances.speaker: Witness VGD23 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not me. He said it -- "you," plural, he was addressing the public at large, meaning Serbs, that Serbs had killed his brother, and his brother was killed and I learned about his brother, I mean that he had been killed sometime in 1997, 1998, but he used to work with me in the police station in Visegrad and I guess that was the reason why.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you knew this man's -- you did know this man's brother?

utterances.speaker: Witness VGD23 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1992, he was still a boy. I think he just enrolled the secondary school, so I knew him by sight, yes, I knew him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it seems that you know the circumstances under which his brother was killed; you told us it was 1997, 1998. Do you know the circumstances under which his brother was killed?

utterances.speaker: Witness VGD23 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The circumstances, I do not know them, but he was killed in -- towards the end of 1992 or in 1993. That is something that I learned about in 1997 or 1998 when I came across another colleague, a Muslim, who had come from Sarajevo to Visegrad to get some papers. And he knew that I worked there, so he looked for me. We then went to have a cup of coffee, and he told me that Fikret Podzic had been killed in a battle near Visegrad and that he commanded there a unit which had come from Sarajevo to reinforce the Muslim forces near Visegrad.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And isn't it a fact that this man who recognised you threatened to somehow ascertain when your flight was returning to Sarajevo, and didn't he threaten to meet you somehow after you returned to Sarajevo and harm you? Isn't that a fact?

utterances.speaker: Witness VGD23 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So was any threat made to you if you returned through Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: Witness VGD23 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not directly, although from what he said, "You must thank God that we met here, if it had been elsewhere, then you'd see who was your -- who was your Lord." And that definitely sounded like a threat, but not a definite threat, not a specific threat.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For those of us who aren't all that familiar where Sarajevo airport is, isn't it correct that Sarajevo airport is a matter of maybe 100, 200 metres from the Republika Srpska? It's very close to the border of the Republika Srpska; is that not correct?

utterances.speaker: Witness VGD23 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't say quite exactly yes. Could be 500 metres, a kilometre maybe, 500. Can't be more accurate.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And of all the Serbs that travelled through Sarajevo airport, it's your testimony that this man who works at the airport singled you out for these implied threats and for this verbal attack simply because you are a Serb, that it was addressed not to you personally but to all Serbs in general; is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: Witness VGD23 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, more or less. Not to me directly but I'd been passing through Gorazde, through Sarajevo, before that going to Zenica. I've been moving through the Federation and never had any trouble and never fearing for myself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you kill this man's brother?

utterances.speaker: Witness VGD23 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were given a guarantee, were you not, before you came to testify here that you would not be arrested for anything you might have done in Bosnia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Witness VGD23 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not only I. The lawyers told us that they had got -- obtained guarantees for everybody, that nobody would have any problems between Visegrad and The Hague and The Hague and Visegrad, that we would have absolutely no problems whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who did you ask for such protection?

utterances.speaker: Witness VGD23 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Personally, I did not ask for it from anyone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it your fear that had you not had that guarantee, that you might have been arrested in The Hague and made to face charges for your conduct in 1992?

utterances.speaker: Witness VGD23 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I know that I haven't done anything. Last year -- rather the year before last, during a UN mission, a policeman from my police station went to East Timor on a mission, and I had also applied, but because of my insufficient knowledge of English and that was the principal or one of the principal terms apart from experience to go there; in other words, I knew that I had done nothing and that it would not be difficult for me, that they would be quite all right for me to work with other policemen who are either Muslims or Croats or coming from any other part of the world.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it's your testimony here today that you never sought any such guarantee but it was simply offered to you, it seemed like a good idea and you accepted it; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Witness VGD23 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I took it as something which is -- which comes in the normal course of events, which is regulated, which, in a way, makes part of testimony, and I took it to be established practice and that is it. I didn't ask for anything.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During your time as a police officer in Visegrad, did you ever become aware of police or ex-police officers or perhaps current police officers from the Serbian town of Obrenovac being present in Visegrad?

utterances.speaker: Witness VGD23 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, isn't it a fact that you, just as the accused in this case, both worked with Milan Lukic during the period of spring of 1992 through to the end of the summer of 1992? Isn't it a fact that both of you were associated with Milan Lukic and helped him perpetrate many of the crimes he did on the people, the Muslim people of Visegrad?

utterances.speaker: Witness VGD23 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Re-examination, Mr. Domazet?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour. Re-examined by Mr. Domazet:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. VGD23, good morning. I have a few questions which I would like you to answer related to the questions that Mr. Groome asked you on Friday and today. Let me start with the incident at the airport. Mr. Groome understood your answer, and with respect to the comment you got from the waiter, I think you said that he had said, "You killed my brother." And Mr. Groome understood that to mean you personally. You explained what was meant by that, and that you considered that he meant the Serbs in general, but that the person you knew was a policeman in Visegrad; is that right?

utterances.speaker: Witness VGD23 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel repeat that question, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Domazet.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: You are being asked to repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: We got lost, I gather.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Okay. [Interpretation] I'm not sure what question is being referred to. Just a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: The one you were --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Mr. Domazet mentioned brother and policemen, could that part of it be repeated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Did you get that, Mr. Domazet?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The person who you said died was a policeman and your colleague in Visegrad; is that right?

utterances.speaker: Witness VGD23 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who was the person you mentioned a moment ago when you said that he was fairly young and that you saw him around in Visegrad? Who was that?

utterances.speaker: Witness VGD23 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was his brother, Muhidin, who had made the threats to us at the airport, who had threatened us at the airport.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you were thinking of him when you were speaking about a young person, a boy, whom you knew by sight in Visegrad; is that right?

utterances.speaker: Witness VGD23 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's how I understood the question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Because I thought that you were thinking of the brother who later died, who was later killed, and it wasn't logical in view of the year. Now, his brother, the one who was a policeman, was he somebody your age or younger or older than you?

utterances.speaker: Witness VGD23 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was younger than me, perhaps 10 years younger. I can't say that that is 100 per cent correct, but at least 10 years.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember until when he was in Visegrad working for the police force?

utterances.speaker: Witness VGD23 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Until 1992. When we left the police station, he stayed on working in the police station.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tie that to the time the Uzice Corps left? After the Uzice Corps left, was he still working there or not?

utterances.speaker: Witness VGD23 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he was no longer in Visegrad as far as I know, and the colleagues that I met in 1997 and 1998 say that he left Visegrad for Sarajevo and that he was the commander of an elite unit, as they were called, of the Muslim army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see him from the moment you mentioned about separation and when you were in Visegrad, did you ever see him after that?

utterances.speaker: Witness VGD23 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that, to the best of your knowledge, he died as the commander of a platoon during some fighting around Visegrad. Do you happen to know any more about that, what kind of fighting and what place he was killed at, how he came to be killed?

utterances.speaker: Witness VGD23 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, according to the information I received, he died near the village of Lijeska, which is inhabited by a purely Serb population.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And just one more question in that area, although I think that you have already answered it, but in view of the direct questions you were asked, whether the information you received told you that he was killed in battle or was he liquidated or rather killed in some other way?

utterances.speaker: Witness VGD23 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He died in battle during the attack on the front line, the defence line, defending the village of Lijeska.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When the front lines that you mention are concerned, as you have explained that you worked in the field in the spring of 1992, can you explain to us what those lines were? Were there contacts between the two sides? Was it a front line and war and fighting between the two sides or something else? What did you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: Witness VGD23 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I meant the people providing security for the village, defending it from possible attack.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So when you say "line," are you thinking of a demarcation line between the Serb and Muslim forces of any kind?

utterances.speaker: Witness VGD23 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, more or less that would be it. A little -- a line is the demarcation line. The delineation line was further in, further in depth, whereas he was killed between the demarcation line and that village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, I understand, but I was asking you generally about demarcation lines as you were in the field and probably had to pay attention to where the Serb forces were located and where the Muslim forces were located. So was there a rule? Was it linked to villages, Serb villages or Muslim villages, or were those lines independent of that at that time, and I'm speaking about the spring of 1992 and the Visegrad environs, of course?

utterances.speaker: Witness VGD23 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the spring of 1992, the lines were around those ethnic areas.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you happen to know what was going on or, rather, what happened if a village exclusively populated by Muslims or a majority of the Muslim population was within the line that, conditionally speaking, belonged to Serb forces, that is to say which was not under the control of Muslim forces? Were there cases of that kind where Muslim villages were in Serb-controlled areas?

utterances.speaker: Witness VGD23 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you personally happen to know -- did you personally see or hear that in villages of this kind, despite such a situation, that the population, the men, male population, able-bodied men, did they stay in the villages, did they remain in the villages, able-bodied men?

utterances.speaker: Witness VGD23 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I personally don't know about that, but most of them, when the reservoir of the hydroelectric power plant, the water was released, fled to Gorazde, went to Gorazde or some other places like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There were several questions relating to your function in the police force before that period and during that period. I don't think you explained sufficiently what your job in the police force was and what you did up until the outbreak of the war.

utterances.speaker: Witness VGD23 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Up until the outbreak of the war, I was the [redacted] [redacted] in the police station of Visegrad.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did that mean to be the [redacted] in the Visegrad police station?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does that mean that up until then, you personally had no function or post in the struggle against crime; you had nothing to do with criminals, their detention and arrest, or anything of that kind, anything outside the realm of traffic and traffic accidents and road safety?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were also asked about the detention and taking into custody of people at that time. Did Visegrad have a court before the war and later on?

utterances.speaker: Witness VGD23 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Visegrad did have a court, a basic court, and a misdemeanours court.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you happen to know that in cases where the court would prescribe detention for a certain case, and in other cases where the law provided for custody and detention, were those -- where were those facilities provided for? Did Visegrad have a prison or a detention centre before the war, before 1992?

utterances.speaker: Witness VGD23 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it did not. Individuals who were taken into custody were sent to the central prison in Sarajevo, where they were incarcerated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So up until 1992, if anybody was detained according to the -- detained according to the law, these individuals were sent to Sarajevo because Visegrad had no detention unit; am I reading you correctly?

utterances.speaker: Witness VGD23 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that possible in 1992 as well, was it possible to do that from April, May onwards? Do you happen to know was it possible to do that at that time, too?

utterances.speaker: Witness VGD23 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it was not possible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know whether a detention unit was set up of any kind in the Visegrad area because of the prevailing situation?

utterances.speaker: Witness VGD23 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You spoke, sir, about a situation in which during those days when the Visegrad dam, when the threat was made to the Visegrad dam, a group of policemen was arrested by the Muslim side. Now, I should like to ask you to take a look at the list you have before you and look at D22.1, that is the list, and tell us whether those people are on the list and, if so, who those people were for whom you know were detained at the time, because I think you said you saw them later on?

utterances.speaker: Witness VGD23 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. VGD10, VGD17, VGD18.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In answer to the question, you said that you saw these people after that. Can you describe what they looked like?

utterances.speaker: Witness VGD23 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can. I saw them straight after they were freed. Their -- they looked terrible. Their hair was all cut, they were disfigured, their bodies were black and blue. You could see visible marks of abuse and everybody was able to see that later on, all those people who watched television and followed this incident through the media, they could all see that for themselves.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness VG61, whom you mentioned as being a man who was in Medjedja, he said here in court that he only saw VG10 of the people after they had been released and that he hadn't been injured in any way nor was anything, any injuries noticeable. Now what you said a moment ago, does that refer to the person on the list under VG10? Does that apply to him, too?

utterances.speaker: Witness VGD23 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it applies to him, too, and if I may say so, in my opinion, he had the worst signs on him and he was probably the person who was -- had been most abused compared to the others, but none of them -- I think there were 12 of them, all of them looked terrible and had signs of mistreatment all over their bodies, marks. They had bruises and they were black and blue and had other types of injuries and they were all -- all their hair had been cut short, and they said that they were threatened, that -- and they had to cut each other's hair, and one of them had the sign of the cross shorn into his hair.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they tell you where they had been incarcerated?

utterances.speaker: Witness VGD23 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they told me. First of all, they were held in the police station, and then later on in the silo belonging to the Gika [phoen] Company. After that, they were kept prisoner in the basement, the cellar in the hydroelectric power plant. I don't know how to refer to this area, but they were where the machinery was kept and there was water flooding in up to their knees. So they spent the whole night standing in a pool of water, and they were interrogated and ill-treated and tortured and that kind of thing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I have one more question about that: Do you know where they were arrested and why?

utterances.speaker: Witness VGD23 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. They were arrested in the village of Nikitovici, in -- at the time when they were patrolling the settlement. It's a Serb settlement, and there was seven of them in the group. They were taken prisoner in a house belonging to a man called Nikitovic and with the seven of them, five others were taken away, five other people who happened to be in the village at the time, Serbs, of course, so that there were 12 of them in all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In answering the question about what job you did at the time, what your function and post was, you said that you were in town rarely, those were your words, and that you, as you said, ensured security for road communications. Did that job have anything to do with the work you had previously done in the traffic department or did you have additional assignments and functions to perform during that time?

utterances.speaker: Witness VGD23 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I understood my job to be the kind of work that I had done previously. I was asked to do the job precisely because of the experience I had gained previously in the work that I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you spoke about the convoy whose escort you were, and when you answered questions about that and you were asked to say what role you played, on Friday, you mentioned the names of several people and I assume that they were in the bus that you escorted. Did I understand that correctly?

utterances.speaker: Witness VGD23 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you understood that correctly. And I do believe that when we meet up, when I meet those people again, if I ever have occasion to do, and I hope I will meet them again, I will be very happy to, and I'm sure they will be happy to see me again. I'm sure that they will at least thank me for the risk that I took, I and my colleagues and, of course, the drivers - I mustn't forget them - for the efforts we invested and the risks we took to ensure their security.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can I take it then that you consider that all those people, if they were to testify about what happened, would testify that you truly were there just to protect them and that you did not abuse that job of protection; is that what you mean when you referred to those people?

utterances.speaker: Witness VGD23 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am profoundly convinced that, quite literally, all of the people from the convoy would testify in the interests of truth and would confirm my statement, and I think that the quotation from the alleged statement could not, I am deeply convinced, could not have been given any of the passengers from the convoy. I'm quite sure of that because I know, and they know, how much we risked to ensure a safe journey, to ensure that their journey would have no problems. If a statement does indeed exist, it could only have been made by somebody who was not present, who was not there at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So all the people in the convoy that you mention, they were all Muslims; is that right?

utterances.speaker: Witness VGD23 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I meant the Muslims. I meant the 250 or perhaps more, give or take a few. Without exception, they would say that, at least that is my conviction; that is what I think. I think all of them without conviction [as interpreted] would confirm what I have said. They would stand by what I have said.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. VG23, I have no further questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you, sir, for coming to give evidence and for the evidence which you have given. You are now free to leave.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, too, for giving me the opportunity of coming here to testify. May I just say that I felt very uncomfortable in certain portions because some people were accusing me of having done things that I could never do. Thank you once again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: There's no point in starting the next witness now, but Mr. Domazet, have you got somebody to fill in for the Friday of this week or for the latter part of the Friday of this week?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the next witness will be Ilija Zecevic, who was to have been heard earlier. He came last Thursday and then he was heard on -- in order to be heard on Friday but he wasn't heard, so that we have shifted the schedule somewhat. But if we get through the witnesses quicker today and tomorrow, then, together with the Victims and Witness Unit, I will ensure that on Friday, we do have more witnesses in addition to the ones that I have listed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, we're very grateful to you for that. I must say the list of witnesses for last week which I received has no reference to Mr. Zecevic. Perhaps there was an amended one which I didn't receive. Very well, then, well, we'll return at 11.30 for the purposes of hearing your next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Now, sir, would you please make the solemn declaration in the document which the court usher is handing you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Sit down, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tanaskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TANASKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Examined by Mr. Tanaskovic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: ILIJA ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To begin with, will you please tell us your full name?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Ilija Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And your date of birth is and where were you born?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I was born on the 20th of October 1951 in the village of Pretisa, in the municipality of Visegrad.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Since when have you been living in Visegrad?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I was been living in Visegrad since 1972 or so, I mean in the town itself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what education do you have?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I came out of the secondary catering hostelry school. I am a waiter by profession.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us where and when did you complete that?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In 1973 in Novi Sad.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Will the counsel and witness please make a break between question and answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Both of you, please, would you pause, counsel, before the question is asked and, witness, before the answer is given to allow the interpreters to catch up. Is the screen showing the transcript in front of the witness? Sir, you will see there the -- on the screen, the transcript, albeit in English, being typed. That will give you some idea of when the translation which we are receiving in English and French has finished. So please wait until you see the typing has finished before you give your answer, and Mr. Tanaskovic, you know how to do it, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TANASKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So tell us, when did you get your first job and where? Did you hear my question?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I heard it, but I'm -- my first job with the Panos Visegrad in 1981.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And until when did you work there?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I worked there until the conflict, right up to the conflict. I worked there until the conflict broke out in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us, how many and which facilities does this Panos hostelry have?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The Panos company, in 1981, had several facilities: Panos restaurant, Visegrad Hotel, Bikovac Hotel, Vilina Vlas hotel, Mesaline restaurant, Pruga restaurant, Grill place, then Express, a fast food restaurant, but then it split in 1984 into a company called Tourism and Vilina Vlas hostelry, so that Valina Vlas and Stara Banja [phoen] became the rehabilitation centre called Valina Vlas, and all the other facilities were under Panos hostelry company.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Of these facilities, could you tell us in which ones of them did you work mostly? Now I have to ask you, will you please wait for me to finish my question, to avoid further warnings by the Court.

utterances.speaker: ILIJA ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I mostly worked in the Visegrad Hotel. It was only when there would be some big parties or when I would be standing in for somebody who was on holidays, then I would work in the Dobrun restaurant. When the staff was on holidays, then I would be there or I worked at Vilina Vlas , for instance, on New Year's Eve or on various other occasions, and I also worked in the Pruga restaurant which was at the bus terminal.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me ask you now, do you know Mr. Mitar Vasiljevic?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I know Mr. and colleague Mitar Vasiljevic very well since 1972 because we attended the school in Novi Sad together, that is, in 1970, I was in Novi Sad and he was in Split. But then there was some complication in Yugoslavia so that students from Split were tranferred to Novi Sad or to Subotica, so that Mitar Vasiljevic and I and some other colleagues of other ethnic ethnicities were together with us. There was a class of cooks, another one of waiters and a third one of bakers. We had some Ramiz Gushki with us, Nastko Sulkic, Milan Kosimitz, Ismet Murtic. We lived in a hostel and were on the same floor, even those were rooms for three so that is in some rooms there were three students sleeping, in others four, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From what you just told us, it means that with all those you mentioned, including Mr. Vasiljevic, you graduated, you completed your training as a waiter that year; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A while ago, you said that you know Mr. Vasiljevic as a colleague too, as a fellow waiter. Now, my question is: Does that mean that Mr. Mitar Vasiljevic also worked as a waiter?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mitar Vasiljevic was a waiter from 1974 onward until those things began to happen in Bosnia-Herzegovina, as I said. He worked for the Panos company in Visegrad and I already said that it was in 1981, that is after him that I joined that company. We worked together. There were other colleagues, those who had been our school fellows in Novi Sad, Subotica and Split, but not all of them. Some others left. One of them became a well-known athlete, but majority of these people came back and worked for our company.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To make it quite clear, it means that Panos is a company from -- with its seat in Visegrad; is that it, a Visegrad-based company; is that it?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us, during that period of time of, say, while you worked for Panos, how large was the staff; how many people did Panos employ, on the average?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I am not able to give you an exact number, but it was about 260 to 280 employees.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your view, if we look at the ethnic structure, how many Serbs were there, how many Muslims, how many others?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I think about 40 per cent were employees of Serb ethnicity, and 60 per cent were Muslims.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I suppose that being colleagues, not only Mr. Mitar Vasiljevic but others, you also socialised, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA ZECEVIC
utterances.text: As people working for Panos company, we were inseparable, at work; we also socialised. We visited one another, visited, that is, our Muslim colleagues and they came to our homes. We never made any distinction between the two. We'd go to Mitar Vasiljevic's place. We were there to mark the birth of his son and other birthdays, and we also visited other colleagues. I don't know how to put it. Whether a Muslim or a Serb, a waiter would, for instance, pay for all that we had to obtain and then we would share it or we would all sign it. We all -- one of the colleagues would keep all the money and we would split amongst us. If there was something left over, that is, if we were given some tips, then we would sit down and spend it all together as we were want to do. After work, we would go to some perhaps private outlets and have a drink, sing, make merry, or sometimes we would come back to my home and there drink and sing after hours or we would go to a Muslim colleague of ours, to Meho Dzafer. Also we'd go to his place, sometimes they would come to our place. Sometimes we went to them and they came to our places. We never made any distinction whether it was a Muslim or a Serb, Meho, Alija, whatever, there was never any separation, never any differentiation. I or other Muslims, we got along very well like brothers both at work and out of work, in the street, or when we would have time off, sometimes we would come to our working place to just socialise, to have a drink and things like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A moment ago what you explained, one purse, one wallet, when you say you were all on one wallet that we don't have to go into that because I do not think it is all that important, and I think you explained that because it wasn't quite clear what you meant when you said one wallet, that you all worked from one wallet or with one wallet. You said that you also went to see Mr. Mitar Vasiljevic at his home. Could you tell us how often that was? Was that often or was it only once that you went to his home and what were the occasions on which you visited with him?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA ZECEVIC
utterances.text: We visited Mr. Mitar Vasiljevic a number of times, I don't know how many, once, twice, three times, depending on the company we were in, where we were sitting, where we socialised, the mood and possibilities and whether perhaps somebody would not be free to go because at times we had to work until midnight or half past 12.00 at night, or perhaps somebody's wife would be ill or a child, that he'd have to go home, that is, he simply could not invite us. But whoever was free and did not have any problems, he'd invite us and we'd go to him and we all sit together. But we all went in a bunch. We were always happy, enjoyed our company. We were always very hospitable, whether it be at his place or at my place or somebody else's place. And the merriment and the party would go on and on and on. I don't know how to put it. We'd stay together, enjoy ourselves as long as we felt like it, and talk and then we'd part company. If somebody had a car, then he'd give a lift to somebody else, whether it be a Serb or a Muslim. For instance, if I had a car, then I'd take a Muslim home or perhaps if a Muslim colleague had a car and I didn't have my car with me, then he'd give me a lift and take me home. So that we always helped one another. We always were there to help whoever needed any help.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Do you think we could move on to what is in issue in this case?

utterances.speaker: MR. TANASKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You talk about these parties, about these binges. When it comes to Mr. Mitar Vasiljevic, what parties were there, if you attended any of those? What occasion were those parties?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Once, I remember we went when his son Nikola was baptised and also his birthday, that is, he invited us two or three days in advance because he said he would mark that, that all his relatives would be there and his neighbours, and he also invited his fellow workers to be there at the party. So depending on whether we were off at that time, those, that is, who did not work at the time because, of course, some had to work and others had to go and attend at the baptism. Say, for instance, it was at 12.00 or at 2.00, for instance, so that those who did not work, those who had their hours off, and I could give you the names of colleagues who were there. It was Meho Dzafic, Medo Dzafic, Omer Koric, Ibrahim Koric, Senad Sabanovic, Ismet Karcic, myself, Nedzip Hadzic; he was the maitre of the hotel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Tanaskovic, we really must move on. Can't you lead him to what it is you want him to give evidence about? We can't have a description of every party they've been to. Please take him to the particular event that you want him to describe.

utterances.speaker: MR. TANASKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've just told us -- I apologise, yes, I'm about to move to that. You told us that you knew Mr. Vasiljevic both as a waiter and as somebody who lived in Visegrad like you. You also said that you socialised, that you drank together. Now, one thing is -- that I want to know, are you aware that Mr. Vasiljevic would sometimes get drunk on such occasions?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vasiljevic would get drunk on such occasions and make merry endlessly. He was really a merry fellow. He loved the company. He did not like to be alone. He liked to have lots of people around him, and he would make merry until he could -- until one could afford, that is, financially, if he couldn't afford it outside, then he'd invite people home so that we would proceed then to his house so we could go on making merry, drinking. He was very sociable, very hospitable. He was not aggressive either when drunk or sober. I don't know what else I can say about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, we'd like to know whether on those occasions or on any other occasion, if you can remember during that period of time when you worked together, did Mr. Vasiljevic ever have any words with any of his colleagues at work, especially, I mean, colleagues of Muslim ethnicity, any quarrel, any bones to pick with?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vasiljevic never had any problems at work, either with his male colleagues or female colleagues or with head waiters or with his bosses or with managers. He never ran into any trouble with anyone and nobody could hold any grudge against him. I have already said that every waiter, every waitress, every cook, every barman, every barmaid trusted him, and me and everybody else who worked there, absolutely no words, no falling out. We always shielded one another regardless of ethnicity. There was absolutely no difference between us, especially when it comes to the ethnic origin. We never had any manifestations of hate.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, will you please be shorter. Try to give us short answers especially to these questions; there is no need. My question is: Where were you in May and June 1992?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In June 1992, the 13th of June, 1992, I was organised in the barracks at Uzamnica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The transcript says, I think you said June of 1992, and my question was where were you in May and June 1992?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I apologise. This is my first time to be here, possibly that I said that, but the truth is that on the 13th of May, I was engaged at the barracks in Uzamnica and in late May and in June, I was again in the barracks at Uzamnica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And from that day on, on the 13th of May, as far as you know, it was still the Yugoslav army, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what were you doing at Uzamnica?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The Territorial Defence had organised us to take -- to look after the barracks before -- after departure, that is, that we should take over and guard the barracks and that I should prepare the food and feed those soldiers who were in the barracks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when the Uzice Corps left, did you stay on?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what did you do then?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: You are both not pausing. Please pause before the answer and before the question. You should ask the question again now, Mr. Tanaskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TANASKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when the Uzice Corps left, my question was whether you stayed on at Uzamnica?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what did you do?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In the kitchen, I distributed food.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us, who did you distribute the food to?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Soldiers who were like me, engaged at Uzamnica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what were those soldiers doing at Uzamnica then?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Those soldiers were assigned there as guards, as keepers of depots and the barracks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say you were a cook. Tell us, did you also prepare the food and distribute it?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I neither cooked nor distributed food. The food came from the command, and I only, when ordered, gave the food to -- served the food to the soldiers in the canteen, or if somebody had been detained in the detention unit, that is, they would ask for a meal for him and I would only pour it out. That is I only poured food out into bowls or plates, and they would then take this food, to whom and where, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say if somebody was in detention. Does that mean that there was also a detention facility there?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, soldier's rooms and a storage room was turned into a detention facility because there was no other facility in Visegrad.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us, before the war, was there a detention facility or a prison in Visegrad?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In Visegrad, before the war, in Visegrad there was a night-time, I think, detention facility at the police station for one person. There was no prison. There were prisons in Foca and Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, that prison for one night in the police station, I'm not sure I know what that means. Could you explain that?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA ZECEVIC
